questions.stem: A technician explains an issue to a non-technical user. Instead of 'the DHCP scope is exhausted,' what should they say?

choices.text: 'The TCP handshake failed on port 67'
'We're freeing up space for more devices to connect'
'Your APIPA lease has expired'
'The subnet mask is misconfigured'

questions.explanation: Avoid jargon - you are the translator between the technical world and the client. Plain language like 'freeing up space for more devices' communicates the idea without confusing the user.
questions.trap: The other options just swap one piece of jargon for another, which is exactly what you should avoid with a non-technical user.

questions.stem: Using the LAST-style active-listening guidance, what is the core habit a technician must STOP doing?

choices.text: Taking notes
Asking probing questions
Interrupting the customer
Clarifying the issue

questions.explanation: We have a bad habit of interrupting because we think we know the answer. Stop interrupting - listen to the entire story, ask probing questions, and take notes.
questions.trap: Note-taking, probing questions, and clarifying are all GOOD listening behaviors; interrupting is the one to stop.

questions.stem: Why should a technician repeat the issue back to the customer 'like a mirror'?

choices.text: To fill time while thinking of a fix
To confirm both parties understand the problem the same way
To show off technical vocabulary
To avoid having to take notes

questions.explanation: Clarifying by repeating the issue back ensures you and the customer share the same understanding of the problem.
questions.trap: Mirroring is about mutual understanding, not stalling or showing off jargon.

questions.stem: A technician is running late to an appointment. What is the professional thing to do?

choices.text: Say nothing and hope the customer doesn't notice
Cancel the appointment entirely
Arrive late and blame traffic
Call ahead to let the customer know

questions.explanation: Be on time; if you are going to be late, call. Proactive communication respects the customer's time.
questions.trap: Staying silent or making excuses on arrival damages trust; calling ahead is the professional move.

questions.stem: How should a technician handle a difficult or upset customer?

choices.text: Educate them without being judgmental, rather than being defensive or argumentative
Argue back to establish authority
Ignore them until they calm down
Escalate immediately to avoid dealing with them

questions.explanation: With a difficult customer, don't be defensive or argumentative - be a teacher and educate them without judgment.
questions.trap: Arguing or ignoring the customer escalates conflict; the goal is calm, non-judgmental education.

questions.stem: A repair will take two weeks. According to 'expectation is reality,' what should the technician do?

choices.text: Tell the customer it'll be done tomorrow to keep them happy
Say nothing until it's finished
Tell the customer the two-week timeline upfront
Quietly extend the deadline as needed

questions.explanation: Manage expectations: if a repair takes two weeks, tell them upfront and communicate status proactively so they don't feel forgotten.
questions.trap: Underpromising a fake short timeline guarantees disappointment; honesty upfront sets the right expectation.

questions.stem: What does the review recommend regarding a technician's attire on the job?

choices.text: Attire doesn't matter as long as the work is good
Dress professionally (formal or business casual) to set the tone
Always wear a full tuxedo
Wear whatever the customer is wearing

questions.explanation: Your attire is your uniform - whether formal or business casual, dress professionally because it sets the tone.
questions.trap: Dismissing attire as irrelevant ignores the professional impression it creates; the standard is professional dress.

questions.stem: Which behavior counts as avoiding distractions during a customer interaction?

choices.text: Taking personal calls and texting while working
Checking social media between steps
Refraining from texting and personal calls while with the customer
Watching videos on your phone during the repair

questions.explanation: Avoid distractions like texting or personal calls while you're with the customer; give them your full attention.
questions.trap: Texting, social media, and videos are exactly the distractions to avoid - not examples of avoiding them.

questions.stem: When offering a customer repair-or-replace options, what should the technician do?

choices.text: Decide for them without explanation
Only ever recommend the most expensive option
Refuse to give options to avoid liability
Explain the pros and cons of each option clearly

questions.explanation: Offer clear repair or replacement options and explain the pros and cons of each so the customer can make an informed choice.
questions.trap: Deciding for the customer or pushing the priciest option undermines trust; lay out the trade-offs and let them choose.

questions.stem: After completing a job, why should a technician follow up with the customer?

choices.text: To verify satisfaction and catch any small issues that slipped through
To upsell additional unrelated products
To close the ticket without the customer's input
Following up is unnecessary once the fix is done

questions.explanation: Follow up after the job to verify satisfaction; this catches any small issues that may have slipped through the cracks.
questions.trap: Follow-up is about confirming the fix worked, not upselling or skipping the customer's confirmation.
